newsitem.title: UK: International LPG steady ahead of Saudi CP price.
newsitem.headline: International LPG steady ahead of Saudi CP price.

text.p: International liquefied petroleum gas prices were stable this week with the market still catching its breath after the huge price falls at the start of the month.
And many players expect the March Saudi Contract Price (CP), the benchmark against which most LPG east of Suez is based, to be between $50 and $70 a tonne below the February CP.
With further huge price cuts potentially to come, buyers are deferring purchases wherever possible, dealers said.
In the Asian market, trade was effectively stymied by the anticipation of lower March prices. Buyers are keeping off the market, said one Japanese trader.
"All the players are very slow movers, and even though there is some requirement, nobody is moving," he said.
"According to my calculations, from a macro viewpoint there should be some demand but from a micro viewpoint there isn't".
Some Japanese buyers expect a March CP of $250 for propane and butane, down from $320 for propane and $305 for butane now.

While this would represent a sharp fall, it would still make LPG expensive in East Asia compared with Europe. The CP represents a price fob Saudi Arabia, so freight has to be added to reach a cif Japan price. By contrast, propane is valued at around $250 cif Northwest Europe at present.
Demand is also subdued in India, China and Korea. Recent Chinese Lunar New Year celebrations failed, as many had hoped, to provoke a rush for product as stocks were already adequate.
And the death this week of Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping failed to impact on the market. "At this moment I can't see any significant change," said a trader.

There was some activity in the Middle East Gulf this week. Trade sources said 5,000 tonnes of propane traded at CP -$11 a tonne; 8,300 tonnes of propane with the same volume of butane at CP -$16; and 5,000 tonnes of propane at CP -$20, all fob Gulf.
European activity was extremely thin, partly because many in the industry had converged on London for Institute of Petroleum (IP) Week.

A 9,000 tonne propane cargo sold at $266 a tonne cif Lavera or $260 cif Le Havre/Donges, and the narrow price differential between the two options was explained by the vessel being already in the Spanish Mediterranean at the time of the trade. This meant that travelling to Lavera was only a minor detour on the return journey to the North Sea.
But the seller of this piece doubted $260 was now repeatable in NWE, with buyers coming from below $250 and some length seen in the market in early March, further depressing levels.

A cargo of butane was reported sold into the French Mediterranean at $310 cif Lavera, the high level taking some by surprise. The seller added that bids were now heard coming from $300 against offers above $310, but he agreed that trade and discussion had been extremely slow because of IP Week.
The comparative strength of the Mediterranean over NWE has opened a possible arbitrage opportunity between these centres, but there is little other arbitrage opportunity seen.
"On a spot basis it's not working from Europe to the U.S., and doesn't seem to be working to South America either," said a trader. "Interest is mainly in the Med".

In the U.S., propane stocks fell by 2.2 million barrels in the week to February 14, falling below the normal range for the first time since December 1996, according to the Energy Information Administration.
Most of the draw took place in the U.S. Gulf Coast. But even though the draw was expected, the market failed to react, with prices little moved over the week and trade mostly thin.
-- Sebastian Alison, London Newsroom +44 171 542 6412
